newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's budget seen aiding high-tech shift.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's budget seen aiding high-tech shift.

text.p: Singapore's budget for fiscal year 1997/98 offered few incentives for the business sector as a whole but analysts said on Friday it would aid the shift towards a high technology environment.

Described mostly as a "bland" or "unsurprising" budget, analysts told Reuters the tax incentives offered by Finance Minister Richard Hu in his speech to parliament were helpful to individuals and the financial sector, not business in general.
"It's a Shenton Way budget, a financial sector budget," David Toh, tax director at Coopers & Lybrand Singapore told Reuters, referring to Singapore's equivalent of Wall Street.

"On the corporate side, the bulk of the incentives were given to banks and financial institutions. But most of the incentives are basically extension of what they already got. No dramatic changes," Toh said. "There will be some business sectors in the economy who will be disappointed," he said.

"It was quite disappointing for corporations. I was expecting a one percent (tax) cut to 25 percent. But nothing changed. It was more generous with individuals," said economist Liew Yin Tze of J.M. Sassoon & Co.
The budget left corporate tax rates unchanged at 26 percent but gave a once-off rebate of 10 percent on individual income tax for year of assessment 1997.
To further develop the financial services sector and entrench its role as a regional financial hub, a package of new incentives were announced.

These included extending a five percent tax on incremental income to income derived from all taxable Asian Currency Units (ACU) activities if total taxable income exceed S$50 million. ACUs are accounting units related to trade in non-resident deposits.
Recognising the growing importance of telecommunications in Singapore, a tax exemption from leasing satellites operated by non-resident persons was announced.
An industrial building allowance was granted for buildings owned and used for goods storage by logistics firms.

While disappointed with the unchanged corporate tax rates, analysts agreed the budget with its targetted incentives was necessary for Singapore's long-term shift away from labour-intensive manufacturing sectors -- where competition with other countries is fierce -- to high-value added services and high-technology-based industries.
"They have addressed the core problems. You notice the changes are very specific. The banks, logistics companies are the new areas the government is trying to promote," Toh said.

"There is no doubt what they did to the logistics and satellite business is correct. They must do it if they want to move on to the international line for our economy. They are headed in the right direction."
